summary: Defines the CMS content constraints extension, which says what kinds of protected content a public key may be trusted for. It helps decide whether a digital signature or encrypted message is acceptable when validating.

plainLanguage.summary: A key can have a note that says "only good for signing invoices, not contracts". This defines how to write that note so receivers can check it.

questions: how to limit what a certificate can sign
what is the cms content constraints extension
what does anycontenttype mean in cms
subtitle: A certificate extension that says which kinds of signed content a public key is allowed to vouch for.

tldr.problem: A valid signature does not say whether the signer should be trusted for this kind of content. One key may be fine for firmware packages but not for certificate management messages.
tldr.mechanism: A CMS content constraints (CCC) extension in trust anchors and certificates lists permitted content types, whether the key may be the innermost source, and optional attribute value limits. Each certificate in a path can only narrow what its issuer allowed.
tldr.outcome: A message is accepted only if the signature checks out and a certification path authorizes the signer for the content type. The result also supplies default attribute values for attributes the message omits.

facts.label: Absent extension, default meaning
facts.value: Subject authorized for no content type

today: RFC 6010 is a Proposed Standard published in September 2010, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It relies on RFC 5652 for CMS and RFC 5280 for certificate path validation.

sections.title: Authorization for Signed Content
sections.content:
The Cryptographic Message Syntax (CMS) SignedData construct is used to sign many things, such as cryptographic module firmware packages (RFC 4108) and certificate management messages (RFC 5272). AuthenticatedData and AuthEnvelopedData provide authentication that can be tied to an originator's static public key.

The RFC assumes an authorization model in which each originator is associated with one or more authorized content types. A message is valid only if the signature or message authentication code (MAC) verifies and the originator is authorized for the encapsulated content type. One originator might be acceptable for firmware packages but not for certificate management messages.

Constraints come from the certification path used to validate the key. They are attached to trust anchors (RFC 5914) and optionally to certificates (RFC 5280). Delegation works by issuing a certificate with a suitable CCC extension. A certificate with no CCC extension means the subject is not authorized for any content type.
sections.plainLanguage: A signature proves who sent something. It does not prove they are allowed to send that kind of thing. This RFC adds the missing permission check.

sections.title: CMS Paths, Content Types and Attributes
sections.content:
CMS wraps content in layers, and each layer is identified by an object identifier. The RFC splits content types into two groups. Intermediate content types, such as SignedData or ContentCollection, wrap other content and add a service like a signature. Leaf content types, such as FirmwarePkgData, carry the actual information.

The outermost structure is always ContentInfo. A route from the outermost node to a leaf is a CMS path. A ContentCollection lets the structure branch like a tree, and each path is processed independently of the others, so some leaves in a collection can be acceptable while others are not. CCC processing stops at a MIME encapsulation layer.

Attributes can be asserted at many points in a path, and CMS does not say which element an attribute applies to. CCC therefore collects all authenticated attributes in the path. The RFC chose the strictest of three considered models: every signer must be authorized for all attributes appearing anywhere in the CMS path.
sections.plainLanguage: Think of a parcel with boxes inside boxes. Each box may have its own stamp. The checker opens them in order and makes sure every stamper was allowed to stamp this parcel.

sections.title: The Extension Syntax
sections.content:
The extension is identified by id-pe-cmsContentConstraints. It MAY be critical and MUST appear at most once in a trust anchor or certificate. Its value is a list of ContentTypeConstraint entries. A given content type MUST NOT appear more than once.

Each entry has three parts:

  • contentType: an object identifier for a permitted content type. Intermediate content types MUST NOT be listed, because intermediate nodes are not subject to constraint processing.
  • canSource: either canSource (the default) or cannotSource. It says whether the subject may be the innermost authenticator of that content type. Regardless of the flag, a subject can sign content that is already authenticated.
  • attrConstraints: an optional list of attribute types with permitted values. If present, the key can verify that content type only if all constraints are satisfied. Attribute types not listed are unconstrained.

The special id-ct-anyContentType value authorizes any content type without constraints, and is used in unconstrained trust anchors. A specific content type listed next to it is authoritative. Attributes not covered by the signature or MAC are not checked against constraints.
sections.plainLanguage: The permission slip lists the kinds of documents the key may sign. Each line can add extra rules, such as "only if the document says it is for the red team".

sections.title: Certification Path Processing
sections.content:
CCC processing is added to the certification path validation of RFC 5280, Section 6. Alternative implementations are allowed only if they yield the same results. If no valid certification path is found, the CMS path MUST be rejected.

Two boolean inputs control the edge cases. inhibitAnyContentType decides whether the anyContentType value counts as matching a content type. absenceEqualsUnconstrained decides what a missing extension means: when true, a trust anchor without one is unconstrained and a certificate without one has the same privileges as its issuer; when false, neither is authorized for any content type. Neither flag affects an apex trust anchor, which is always unconstrained.

The algorithm starts with the trust anchor's permitted list in working_permitted_content_types. For each certificate it can only shrink the set: content types not in the certificate's extension are dropped and recorded in excluded_content_types, canSource becomes cannotSource unless both entries allow it, and attribute value sets are intersected. An empty intersection removes the content type.

At the end, if the content type of interest is excluded or missing, validation fails. Otherwise the attribute constraints are checked. Constrained attributes absent from the message are returned as subject_default_attributes.
sections.plainLanguage: Each link in the chain can only take permissions away, never add them. Whatever is left at the end is what the signer may do.

sections.title: Processing a CMS Message
sections.content:
Processing runs per CMS path, from the root node to a leaf, and applies to paths containing at least one SignedData, AuthEnvelopedData or AuthenticatedData node. Countersignatures are not covered. Three things are collected: signer or originator keys, attributes, and the leaf node type.

Every signature or MAC MUST be verified, or the path MUST be rejected. Keys go into cms_public_keys, and authenticated attributes go into cms_effective_attributes. Defaults derived from signer authorizations go into cms_default_attributes, which prevents a signer from avoiding a constraint by leaving an attribute out.

A leaf is either an encrypted leaf (EncryptedData, EnvelopedData, AuthEnvelopedData) or a payload leaf. For an encrypted leaf, processing stops and returns the keys and attributes for use after decryption. For a payload leaf, content type and constraint checking MUST be performed: a certification path is built for each collected key, and the signer closest to the payload must be allowed to source that content type, or the path MUST be rejected.

For a SignedData with several SignerInfo elements, each is treated as the only one, and the content is valid if at least one valid CMS path uses one SignerInfo from each SignedData. Where signers should collaborate, using multiple SignedData contents is RECOMMENDED.
sections.plainLanguage: The checker walks through the layers from the outside in, collects every signer and every label, then checks that the signer closest to the content was truly allowed to make it.

sections.title: Subordination in Trust Anchor Management
sections.content:
The Trust Anchor Management Protocol (TAMP, RFC 5934) does not define an authorization mechanism. CCC can authorize TAMP message signers and delegate their authority. A signer's constraints MUST be greater than or equal to the constraints of each trust anchor in an update, or that update MUST be rejected. Each update in a message is accepted or rejected on its own.

How the trust anchor's constraints are found depends on the operation. For an add they come from the extension in the update. For a remove they come from the stored trust anchor. For a change, both the pre-change and post-change constraints are checked. An unconstrained trust anchor can only be managed by an unconstrained signer.
sections.plainLanguage: A manager can only hand out permissions that the manager already has. This section makes sure of that when trust anchors are added, changed or removed.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Several certification paths may exist for one certificate, and each can give different CCC results, including different default attributes. Compromise of a trust anchor private key lets an attacker produce messages acceptable to every application whose trust anchor store holds the matching trust anchor. For example, a trust anchor authorized for firmware could yield installable malicious firmware.

CCC treats all attributes in a path as applying to the encapsulated content, even though CMS does not say what an attribute applies to. The RFC warns against provisioning constraints on attribute types never used to describe a leaf, such as MessageDigest. When the ESSCertId attribute is used, alternative signer certificates are not permitted, which may cause failures where another certificate would have succeeded.
sections.plainLanguage: If someone steals a powerful key, they can sign anything that key was allowed to sign. Also, labels on a parcel might not say which box they belong to, so be careful which rules you attach to labels.

items.text: Object identifier of a permitted leaf content type. Intermediate types are not listed.

items.title: attrConstraints
